sources.content:
Module 0 exists to front-load every piece of setup friction so that Modules 1 through 30 are pure learning, not troubleshooting.
Why This Topic Matters
In a professional AI Engineering role, your development environment is not a personal preference - it's part of the team's shared tooling. Getting comfortable with virtual environments, API key management, and reproducible project structure from day one builds habits that transfer directly into how real AI engineering teams operate.
Industry Relevance
Companies onboarding AI engineers lose real time to environment setup. Teams that standardize on uv / poetry , .env conventions, and Docker-based local development consistently onboard new engineers faster and have fewer 'works on my machine' incidents - this is why we establish those conventions here rather than later.
Common Misconceptions
'I'll just use a Jupyter notebook for everything.' Notebooks are excellent for exploration but a liability for production code - no proper import structure, hidden state, poor version control diffs. This handbook uses notebooks only where explicitly noted (mostly in early embeddings/RAG exploration) and regular .py modules everywhere else. ·
'API keys can just live in the code while I'm learning.' This habit causes real security incidents - leaked keys committed to public GitHub repos are one of the most common causes of unexpected API bills. We establish .env + .gitignore discipline immediately. ·
'I need a GPU to learn AI Engineering.' Not for this track. AI Engineering (as distinct from ML/LLM Engineering) is primarily about building systems around hosted or API-served models, not training them locally. ·
Learning Objectives
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
Set up a reproducible Python environment for AI projects. 1.
Securely manage API keys using environment variables. 2.
Structure a new AI project following industry-standard conventions. 3.
Verify connectivity to OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google AI Studio APIs. 4.
Set up Docker for later use in Modules 8, 16, and 26. 5.
Push a properly structured project to GitHub with a clean .gitignore and README.

Mentor Evaluation Rubric
Common Mistakes
Treating prompt engineering as 'done' after one successful manual test , rather than validating against a representative golden set. ·
Writing vague prompts and hoping the model infers the intended format -precision in output-format specification is consistently the highest-leverage fix for unreliable prompts. ·
Ignoring prompt injection risk until it causes an actual incident, rather than treating untrusted content with appropriate skepticism from the start. ·
Scattering prompt strings inline throughout the codebase , making them impossible to review, version, or test systematically as the application grows.

Theory
Project Structure at Scale
Module 0 introduced the basic src/ layout. As a project grows, it typically evolves into:
pyproject.toml centralizes dependency management, tool configuration (ruff, mypy, pytest), and packaging metadata in one file, replacing the older requirements.txt + setup.py + setup.cfg sprawl:
[project] name = "app-name" version = "0.1.0" requires-python = ">=3.11" dependencies = [ "fastapi>=0.110", "httpx>=0.27", "pydantic>=2.6", ] [project.optional-dependencies] dev = ["pytest", "pytest-asyncio", "ruff", "mypy", "respx"] [tool.ruff] line-length = 100 [tool.pytest.ini_options] testpaths = ["tests"] asyncio_mode = "auto"
The Testing Pyramid for AI Applications
Classic software engineering describes a testing pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end tests. AI applications add a fourth layer on top: evaluations , which test model-facing behavior probabilistically rather than deterministically. That layer is covered in depth in Module 22 - for now, understand where it sits:
┌─────────────────────┐ │   Evaluations         │   few, slow, probabilistic (Module 22) │   (LLM output quality) │ ├─────────────────────┤ │  End-to-End Tests      │   few, slow, full system ├─────────────────────┤ │  Integration Tests     │   moderate, real DB/API boundaries mocked selectively ├─────────────────────┤ │  Unit Tests             │   many, fast, isolated, deterministic └─────────────────────┘
The key discipline this module teaches: everything deterministic gets a normal unit test.
